question.prompt: Each of \(20\) balls is tossed independently and at random into one of the \(5\) bins. Let \(p\) be the probability that some bin ends up with \(3\) balls, another with \(5\) balls, and the other three with \(4\) balls each. Let \(q\) be the probability that every bin ends up with \(4\) balls. What is \(\dfrac{p}{q}?\)

solutions.explanation:
Every sequence of destinations for the \(20\) throws has the same probability \((1/5)^{20}\). We can therefore compare counts of sequences, and this common probability will cancel.

For specified bin totals \(n_1,\ldots,n_5\), the sequence count is \(20!/(n_1!\cdots n_5!)\): choose which throws went into each bin. For the \(3,4,4,4,5\) totals, there are additionally \(5\cdot4=20\) choices of the bin with \(3\) balls and the different bin with \(5\) balls. Each resulting sequence has just one such pair, so this introduces no double counting.

Consequently
\[
\frac pq=\frac{20\cdot20!/(3!4!4!4!5!)}{20!/(4!4!4!4!4!)}
=20\cdot\frac{4!\,4!}{3!\,5!}
=20\cdot\frac45=\boxed{16},
\]
choice E.
solutions.title: Cancel equal sequence probabilities and factorial counts
